title: Thirty Miles From Paris
narrativeQuestion: How did a German army thirty miles from Paris end up retreating?

chapters.title: Thirty Miles From Paris
chapters.claim: By September 2, 1914 German cavalry were about thirty miles from Paris and the French government left the city.

chapters.title: Six weeks to beat France
chapters.claim: Germany planned to beat France in about six weeks, and France's own offensive in red trousers cost about 27,000 dead on August 22.

chapters.title: The government left. Gallieni stayed.
chapters.claim: Gallieni, ordered to defend Paris, saw that the nearest German army was passing the city rather than attacking it.

chapters.title: Watch the gap open
chapters.claim: Kluck's turns opened a gap of about thirty miles between the German 1st and 2nd Armies, and the British and French advanced into it.

chapters.title: Six hundred taxis
chapters.claim: About 600 taxis carried about 4,000 soldiers, a tiny share of the French force, yet became the battle's most famous story.

chapters.title: The man in the car
chapters.claim: With poor communications, Moltke sent Lieutenant Colonel Hentsch with spoken authority, and two German armies retreated on September 9.

chapters.title: Legend or record?
chapters.claim: Some famous Marne stories are documented and some are later legends.

chapters.title: What the Marne made
chapters.claim: The retreat to the Aisne began trench warfare and a line that ran about 440 miles by November 1914.

chapters.title: Four questions
chapters.claim: Students explain the turn, the taxis, the two documents and whether the battle was a win.
